narrative:
The model predicts you have a 12% chance of failing your final year. While this is not a high probability, it is enough for the school to require you to take remedial courses as a precaution.

The prediction that you might fail is driven mainly by three aspects of your situation. The most influential factor is that you have had no past class failures. Surprisingly, this actually pushes the model toward expecting you to fail. Among students who passed, having zero previous failures is the average, yet in your specific combination of circumstances the model sees the complete lack of any prior academic struggle as a warning sign rather than a strength. 

The second most important influence is your weekly study time. You report studying more than ten hours per week, far above what most successful students do (the majority study only 2–5 hours). While this extra effort should help, the model interprets it as a sign that you are having to work unusually hard to keep up, which pulls the prediction toward failure.

Finally, the fact that you receive extra educational support at school also contributes to the “fail” direction. Only 3.4% of students who passed needed this kind of support, so the model sees it as an indicator that you are already struggling.

To improve, focus on making your study time more efficient rather than simply longer, seek feedback on why the extra support is needed, and talk with your teachers about building steady progress so you no longer need remedial classes next term. (218 words)
